name: Name the feeling
childPhrase: I find the exact word for what I feel. Not just bad. Annoyed? Embarrassed? Let down? Sometimes it's two at once.
practiceScript: Think of one small thing that bugged you this week. Say the first word that comes. Probably bad, or mad. Now find a sharper word. Annoyed? Embarrassed? Left out? Let down? Jealous? Nervous? Pick one. If two fit, say both. Say it out loud: 'I felt embarrassed, and a bit annoyed.' Now give it a number from 1 to 10. That's it. The word is a tool, not a grade.
kidScienceLine: In adult studies, naming feelings helped people feel less upset. We need stronger tests with children aged 8 to 13.
parentReceipt: Torre and Lieberman, UCLA, Emotion Review, 2018, DOI 10.1177/1754073917742706; fit ADULT ONLY for this move. Lieberman, Eisenberger, Crockett, Tom, Pfeifer and Way, UCLA, Psychological Science, 2007, DOI 10.1111/j.1467-9280.2007.01916.x, PMID 17576282; adult brain scans; fit MECHANISM. Nook and colleagues, Harvard, 2018, DOI 10.1177/0956797618773357, PMID 29878880; ages 5 to 25; fit ADJACENT. Starr and colleagues, University of Rochester, 2020, DOI 10.1037/emo0000630, PMID 31246045; 233 teens aged 14 to 17; fit ADJACENT. Naming feelings and telling feelings apart have related but different evidence; none of these papers directly tests this home practice in children aged 8 to 13.

source.text: Torre and Lieberman at UCLA reviewed studies of putting feelings into words in 2018. In adult studies, naming feelings sometimes reduced upset. A 2007 adult brain-scan study found changes in brain activity while people labeled emotional pictures. These findings do not prove that this home practice helps children aged 8 to 13. source.limitation: Adult naming studies do not prove the same benefit in children aged 8 to 13. The child and teen studies measured a related skill without teaching it.

name: Breathe out slowly
childPhrase: I breathe in easily through my nose, then let it out slowly. Three to five times.
practiceScript: Sit back. Breathe in through your nose: one, two, three, four. Now let it out slowly, like fogging a window: one, two, three, four, five, six. Again. In for four. Out for six. One more time. Three is enough. If your head feels funny, stop and breathe normally.
kidScienceLine: In children taking a math test, deep breathing helped them feel less worried. This mixed evidence means we cannot promise it helps in daily life.

source.text: "In Singapore, a scientist at Nanyang Technological University asked 122 kids, about 10 and 11 years old, to take slow deep breaths before a timed math test. name: Talk kindly to yourself
childPhrase: I step back and watch it like a movie. Then I talk to myself by name, like a good coach: '[name], what's the next play?'
practiceScript: Think of a time you got mad at someone. Not the worst one, a medium one. Now picture it from across the room, like you're watching a movie of yourself. Ask: 'Why did [name] feel that way?' Notice what the other person might have been thinking. Now give one coach line, using your own name: '[name], you were annoyed. What's one thing you can do next?'
kidScienceLine: In adults, using their own name during self-talk helped them feel less upset under stress. This adult research does not prove a kind coach line helps children.
parentReceipt: Kross and colleagues, University of Michigan, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 2014, DOI 10.1037/a0035173, PMID 24467424; adult self-talk studies; fit ADULT ONLY. Kross, Duckworth, Ayduk, Tsukayama and Mischel, Emotion, 2011, DOI 10.1037/a0021787, PMID 21728415; fifth graders recalled anger from an outside view; fit ADJACENT for this kind self-talk move. White and colleagues, Child Development, 2017, PMID 27982409; ages 4 and 6, task perseverance; fit ADJACENT. None tests the whole kind coach line with children aged 8 to 13.

source.text: In 2014, Kross and colleagues studied how adults talked to themselves before stressful social tasks. Using their own name and words such as you instead of I helped them feel less upset. This was not a test of kind wording alone or of the whole move with children. The 2011 fifth-grade study tested stepping back to think about anger; the 2017 White study tested younger children staying with a task. Search: self-talk Kross 2014.
source.limitation: Own-name self-talk, visual stepping back and kind wording are different parts of this move. The adult result does not prove the whole child practice helps.

whenNotToUse: the coach is never harsh ("you idiot" is not a coach); never to bury a feeling, name it first; a scary event that really happened goes to Card B.

name: Plan what you'll do
childPhrase: I picture what I want, spot the snag inside me that could stop it, and make a plan: 'If the snag shows up, then I will ___.'
practiceScript: Pick one wish for this week. Say it in a few words: 'Finish math before dinner.' Now picture the best part of getting it done. Really see it. Now find the snag. Not other people. kidScienceLine: In fifth graders, picturing a wish and planning for snags helped improve grades. This school test does not show that the plan helps with feelings.

source.text: "In 2013, Angela Duckworth and Gabriele Oettingen taught 77 fifth graders at a city middle school in the US a trick: picture your wish, spot the snag, then make an if-then plan. In Germany in 2011, kids aged 5 to 8 with an if-then plan ignored a fun video better too." Search: "mental contrasting if-then plans fifth graders".

name: Say sorry and help
childPhrase: When I hurt someone, I say exactly what I did, say sorry without a 'but', and do one thing to fix it. Then I let them answer in their own time.
practiceScript: Think of a small time you upset someone. Name exactly what you did: not 'I was mean', but 'I laughed when you dropped your tray.' Now the sorry, with no 'but': 'I'm sorry I laughed.' Now one fix you can do, not just say: help, replace, write a note, include them next time. Last part: they might not be ready. That's their choice. Your part is done.
kidScienceLine: In children aged 6 to 10, making things right helped them feel less guilty. This pretend mistake does not show what happens after hurting a real friend.

source.text: "In 2019, scientists Meghan Rose Donohue and Erin Tully set up a game in the US where kids aged 6 to 10 thought they had upset another kid. Kids who got a chance to fix it, by giving stickers and writing a note, felt their guilt go down. Kids who had no chance to fix it did not. In China, 180 kids aged 9 and 11 trusted a game partner again after the partner said sorry." Search: "repair guilt children Donohue Tully".
source.limitation: the wrong was pretend, in a lab, with a stranger, not a real friend.

whenNotToUse: when the child was the one hurt (use Bring in my person); never force a sorry while the child is still hot; no groveling and no public sorry; if the other child wants space, the fix waits; anything that harmed someone badly is a grown-up job.
whenItFits: "said something mean to her friend and feels awful"; "broke his brother's thing"; "left a friend out and now feels guilty"; "can't stop thinking about what she did".
positiveAction: Broke someone's pencil? Say sorry and give them another.
